name: Jotunheim-Veil
geological_features: Hydrogen-metallic ocean layer spanning the inner mantle
Counter-rotating storm bands visible across both hemispheres
Supercritical helium rain cascading through the mid-atmosphere
Magnetospheric aurora columns reaching 40,000 kilometers in height
specific_features: Binary sunset created by twin K-type stars casting overlapping orange-crimson shadows across the cloud tops
A shattered moon ring formed from a captured satellite torn apart by tidal forces
Periodic radio bursts emanating from deep within the metallic hydrogen core
description: Jotunheim-Veil is a titan among worlds, a gas giant of staggering proportions that dominates its binary star system like a dark emperor on a throne of storms. Its banded atmosphere churns in ribbons of amber, slate, and bruised violet, counter-rotating at speeds that would shred any vessel foolish enough to descend below the upper cloud decks. The shattered remnants of a captured moon form a pale ring system that catches the light of both suns in a perpetual glittering halo.

Twice each orbital cycle, the twin K-type stars align behind the planet and cast a binary sunset across its face, painting the cloud tops in layered shades of burnt copper and deep crimson. The effect is visible from neighboring worlds and has become a navigational landmark for deep-space pilots crossing the outer territories. In those brief hours of dual twilight, the aurora columns flare to their brightest, turning Jotunheim-Veil into a lantern visible across the system.

Early survey teams designated this world as a fuel depot candidate, drawn by the vast reservoirs of helium-3 suspended in its upper atmosphere. Three separate extraction platforms were constructed in orbit, but two were lost to unexplained electromagnetic surges originating from the planet's core. The surviving platform operates on a skeleton crew, its personnel reporting strange radio patterns that some xenolinguists believe carry structure, though no consensus has been reached.

Jotunheim-Veil remains a prize too valuable to abandon and too dangerous to exploit carelessly. The fuel cartels maintain a tense standoff over harvesting rights, while independent researchers petition for protected study of the core radio emissions. Any faction that could crack the mystery of those deep-layer signals might gain leverage over the entire system, but descending into the crushing pressures below the cloud line has claimed every probe sent so far.
